item.title: The U.S. Army’s Pacific Strategy Depends on Allies
item.description:
“We never fight alone. We've never done that. You can go all the way back to the days of Revolutionary War. The United States has never gone into conflict on its own. We've always built coalitions. We've always involved partners and allies. And we'll continue to do so going forward.”

That was Gen. Ronald P. Clark, Commanding General, U.S. Army Pacific Command, speaking last Tuesday at a contemporary military forum, Decisive Landpower -- Deterrence and Partner Integration Against the Pacing Threat, as part of the 2026 Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Conference in Washington, D.C.

On the panel with Clark was Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, Commander, United Nations Command, U.S. Forces Korea, and Tara Murphy Dougherty, Chief Executive Officer of Air, a leading AI software firm that specializes in national security readiness.

The two Army generals spent a good deal of their time talking about lessons learned from Ukraine and the benefits to the U.S. of allies – specifically in the Pacific. That struck me as something to further explore, since one day later, on Wednesday, President Trump continued his running criticism of allies with an October 14, Truth Social screed.

Trump said in part: “Because of the fact that we have had such Military Success, we no longer ‘need,’ or desire, the NATO Countries’ assistance — WE NEVER DID! Likewise, Japan, Australia, or South Korea. In fact, speaking as President of the United States of America, by far the Most Powerful Country Anywhere in the World, WE DO NOT NEED THE HELP OF ANYONE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

On the other hand, Gen. Brunson had told the AUSA audience one day earlier, “Everything that we do is intricately woven around the ROK (Republic of Korea)-U.S. alliance. That alliance has stood for some 75 years and it is an example or a paragon, if you will, of all that's right when folk work in alliance together. The problems that we solve are joint problems. They're not just U.S. problems. They're not just Republic of Korea problems. What they are is great opportunities for two nations to work in concert with one another in order to arrive at solutions that are beneficial for both countries.”

Gen. Clark explained further, “So our ability to be able to work with partners and allies on their sovereign soil, to be able to share procedures that we build through [military] exercises over the course of a year, some joint, some army-to-army, but always integrated with our partners. It gives us the opportunity to have our systems work technically, to have our procedures nested, and to get to know one another in a way that allows us to build the trust that's necessary in training. Because if we wait until crisis or conflict, it's too late to ask the question, can I trust

you? But because we've been working together, because we've exercised at scale, because we're modernizing our forces alongside one another, it works.”

Clark added, “We've really worked hard at building those relationships at scale inside of the land forces. We have a land forces dialogue that meets multiple times a year -- chiefs of army of Australia, Japan, the Philippines, and the U.S. We've invited the ROKs in, we've invited India in, and it continues to grow. So those relationships built army-to-army are what allows us to really integrate across interoperability, and integrate it really across our formations and with our partners in all.”

Brunson described how he and Korean Gen. Kim Sung-min, Deputy Commander of the U.S.-ROK Combined Forces Command, discussed training differently “taking advantage of the knowledge that we have of the threats that exist or that prevail in the Ukraine fight.”

Brunson said, “We talk about how we would operate in a distributed fashion…Just imagine if we trained across the entirety of the [Korean] Peninsula and got ourselves in a shape where we would say you can't utilize the things that you've learned in the fight in the battlefield in Ukraine on us, because we learned the same lessons and we've distributed ourselves in such a way that we don't make ourselves the target. We won't be moored in place.”

Clark talked about Russia, North Korea and China “learning from watching us partner, but the partnerships that our adversaries have built are transactional versus the transformational relationships that we build as a security partner of choice globally…for us it's really transformational relationships that we look to cultivate with partners and allies over time.”

Brunson described how the North Koreans, fighting for the Russians in Ukraine were “able to test systems there…and then bring that back home. So, in one aspect, they've shortened their RDT&E cycle.” He also pointed out, “The fact that you have a combat trained force with recent

combat on the [Korean] Peninsula for the first time since 1953..[and] are now bringing those lessons learned back into their own training cycle, it's shortened their time to develop them.”

Clark said that U.S. forces had also learned from Ukraine about the need for mobility and camouflage, which he described as “age-old army forgotten sciences of how to hide in plain sight and how to camouflage ourselves from observation...Our ability to be able to use electronic warfare, to be able to use just good, old-fashioned camouflage and the ability to deceive our adversary is a must. In those two theaters [Ukraine and Iran] it's not a near-peer adversary that we would be working against -- whereas, in our theater [the Pacific] it absolutely is.”

For Clark, the questions were: “How do we fight, you know, Type One, Type Two UAS [unmanned aerial system, drones]; how do we think through ballistic missile defense holistically in the region. We spend a lot of time working again with the joint force for solutions associated with that. How do we maneuver?”

Brunson raised a new issue by pointing out that, “Our old system was something [a weapons system] breaks, we send it all the way back CONUS [Continental U.S.] in order to fix it so we can then bring it all the way back out again.” That used to take 29 days by ship.

However, he added, “In the ally that we have in Korea we have a an absolutely premier industrial base, if you look at the Korea defense industry, some of the kit that we're producing right now sits along our friends, allies and partners.” Brunson said, “The Army’s new infantry squad vehicle (ISV), for example, is produced by GM Defense and GM Defense is also in the Republic of Korea.”

“So the idea of a regional sustainment hub would simply be…to bring those means of production to the theater,” Brunson suggested, noting, “In the maritime domain, when we look at maintenance, repair, and overhaul, which is being done forward alongside the Koreans, you know that 15 percent of global ship building is done in Korea. And, oh by the way, we've got an ally with a mutual defense treaty in Japan that has 10% of global ship building. And if we take these cases forward, we're able to stay in theater longer.”

The answer, Brunson said, “We've got to try to achieve admirable endurance in theater by partnering alongside our allies, seeing the things that they can do better than we can right now at distance and then keeping them right where they belong. That keeps our [military] forces forward.”

Dougherty chipped in saying: “Tens of millions of dollars saved by simply identifying things like unfilled requisitions or parts that are obsolete that can be replaced with something not obsolete and also less expensive. I think that this is it. This is part of how you generate lethality. You get readiness to pay for itself, because otherwise sustainment is too expensive when it has to be done for the entirety of the joint force all the way on the other side of the world.”

At one point, Clark said, “The secret sauce for us as an Army is our Non-Commissioned Officer (NCO) corps, reflecting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s September 30 speech praising the same group.

Clark noted that both he and Brunson were sons of NCOs, and that “with the assistance of our senior non-commissioned officers, senior enlisted leaders across the [PACOM] region have embarked upon conducting assessments with our partners and developing strategies to help them build their NCO development programs inside of their formations.”

To illustrate his point, Clark said his units had just finished an assessment in Cambodia of its army and the Commander, Gen. Mao Sophan, “basically said, ‘Hey, whatever you're asking us to do, we're going to do it because we want to get to a level of proficiency with our Non-Commissioned Officer core that we see in yours.’"

I must point out that during the one-hour-and-thirty-minute session neither General -- Clark nor Brunson -- came near to mentioning President Trump’s repeated critical views about U.S. allies.

The closest anyone came was Dougherty, who at one point said diplomatically, “We'll head into midterm elections here [in the U.S.] in November, obviously as you know, and I think we expect some variation in the political dynamic in the United States, and our allies and partners all navigate their own political changes as well.”

She then added, “If you look over the course of history, however, at least modern history, certainly the United States has invested in those partnerships. And today, we still are -- maybe with a different flavor or a different attitude. And that's not really for me to say. I'm simply observing. But we haven't lost sight of the importance of allies and partners to securing U.S. national interests.”

I would bet Clark and Brunson – along with most U.S. military professionals – would silently agree with her statement.

item.title: The Hidden Risks of AI-Powered Intelligence
item.description:
Picture an intelligent analyst's screen. Data about troop movements, a port closure, a terrorist attack, or a weapons transfer sits at the center of a clean interface, with a confidence indicator glowing green. Two hundred outlets are carrying it, and the platform has counted every one. It looks like a corroboration. In many cases, it is a single Telegram post, copied, translated, summarized, and republished until its origin disappeared behind its own echo.

Nobody must be negligent for this to happen. It is what you get when a product or platform is built to measure volume and the user is tempted to read volume as truth.

I say this as someone who works with open-source material and believes in it. Commercial imagery, ship-tracking data, procurement records, leaked databases, and social media have changed what is knowable about conflicts and illicit networks; but the market that has grown up around these sources is selling something different from the discipline that makes them valuable, and governments and companies are buying it without noticing the difference.

A Crowded Market and a Thin Product

Open-source intelligence platforms are multiplying quickly. Walk through the company stands at any security conference and you will find dozens of them, each promising to fuse, monitor, and surface threats across the open internet, now almost always with an AI layer that summarizes, ranks, and alerts.

Strip away the interface and most of them offer little that a competent analyst couldn't already do with a search engine, a handful of specialist tools, and some patience. Reverse image searching, scraping social platforms, pulling corporate registry data, and geolocating an image are all learnable skills, and many of the best practitioners picked them up in public, often as volunteers. What the platforms add is convenience and scale, which is genuinely useful, but convenience is not analysis. The real product, in most cases, is the dashboard.

Dashboards are persuasive by design. They squeeze a messy information environment into something that looks like a picture of the world, with counts, trend lines, heat maps, and sentiment scores. Each of those findings implies that someone has already done the hard work of deciding what matters and what is true. Usually, no one has. The system has counted things, and counting is the easy part.

Counting Sources Is Not Testing Them

The core flaw is in what these systems reward. They tend to measure the number of sources behind a claim, not the independence of those sources. The two are very different things.

Independence is the foundation of corroboration. Two witnesses who saw an event separately make a claim stronger. Two witnesses who heard about it from the same third person do not. The same logic applies to reporting. A claim that traces back to a single channel but appears in two hundred outlets has one source and two hundred echoes.

Intelligence tradecraft has a name for this: circular reporting. It is among the oldest and best-documented ways analysts go wrong. The failures that most damaged the credibility of Western intelligence in the past generation involved, among other things, uncorroborated claims that were repeated, cross-referenced, and eventually treated as established because they seemed to come from many places. The lesson drawn at the time was that provenance matters more than prevalence. An aggregator that treats prevalence as confirmation is rebuilding the vulnerability that analysts spent years learning to guard against.

AI makes this problem fourfold. First, language models summarize and synthesize, and in doing so they take away the provenance trail that an analyst needs. A fluent paragraph that blends fifteen sources does not tell you that twelve of them are derivative. Second, the cost of generating plausible content has collapsed. Fabricated articles, cloned news sites, and coordinated amplification networks can now create the appearance of breadth cheaply, which is exactly the signal these platforms are built to count. Third, as more web content is produced or recycled by automated systems, the pool that analytics tools draw from becomes more self-referential. The echo chamber is increasingly populated by machines quoting each other. Lastly, AI can make uncertainty harder to see. Language models are designed to produce coherent answers, not to preserve the ambiguity of the evidence on which those answers are based. Contradictory sources can be reconciled into a smooth narrative, gaps can disappear beneath plausible inference, and tentative conclusions can acquire the tone of established fact. The danger is therefore not simply that an analyst receives false information, but that the uncertainty surrounding otherwise legitimate information becomes less visible.

None of this means the technology is useless. Entity extraction, translation, deduplication, and pattern detection across large data sets are real contributions. But the same tools that can help trace a claim to its origin are too often deployed to certify it instead.

Information Is Not Intelligence

The deeper problem is what happens after the dashboard produces its output. Companies market it as intelligence, and buyers, including government agencies, intelligence firms, financial institutions, and corporate security teams, purchase it as intelligence, then act on it.

However, open-source material is raw information. It becomes intelligence only after a process that no interface can fully automate. Someone has to establish where the material came from, grade how reliable the source has been, assess how credible the specific claim is, and test it against other collection. Established standards exist for this. Grading systems that rate source reliability separately from information credibility have been used for decades, and analytic standards require analysts to describe the quality and credibility of their sources, to distinguish between underlying evidence and judgment, and to account for alternative explanations. These are not bureaucratic formalities. They are the mechanism by which an organization knows how much weight a conclusion can bear.

When that step is skipped, the result is aggregated internet content with a confident interface. The output reads like a finished product, but the epistemic work behind it is missing, and the person reading it often can't see that. A decisionmaker shown a green indicator does not know whether it reflects three independent confirmations or one rumor with good distribution.

The consequences are practical. A government that bases sanctions designations, force posture, or diplomatic messaging on an unverified claim risks embarrassment at best and escalation at worst. A company that reroutes shipments or exits a market because a risk platform flagged a rumor can lose real money; and an agency that comes to rely on commercial feeds may quietly stop investing in the capabilities that would let it check them.


What Should Change

I would offer the following two principles.

One, to treat provenance and independence as essential to intelligence. Open-source material should be treated as a cue and a corroborator, not a conclusion. Open sources are at their best when they point collection in a useful direction or when they test and strengthen what other sources have suggested. A satellite image that shows construction at a site tells analysts where to look and what to ask. A procurement database entry might confirm a pattern already suspected. Neither is a finding on its own. The workflow should run from open-source lead to targeted collection to assessment, not from dashboard alert to briefing slide. As AI makes it easier to summarize, reproduce and generate information, analysts need to know not only what a source says, but where the information originated and whether apparently separate sources are actually independent. A fluent paragraph that blends fifteen sources does not tell an analyst that twelve of them are derivative. Likewise, a cluster of articles, websites or database entries may create the appearance of broad corroboration while ultimately tracing back to a single underlying claim. Platforms should therefore preserve provenance wherever possible and make the distinction between original reporting, derivative content and AI-generated material visible to the user. The workflow should run from open-source lead to targeted collection to assessment, not from dashboard alert to briefing slide.

Two, protect human assessment and the collection that supports it. AI can make uncertainty harder to see. Language models are designed to produce coherent answers, not to preserve the ambiguity of the evidence on which those answers are based. Contradictory sources can be reconciled into a smooth narrative, gaps can disappear beneath plausible inference, and tentative conclusions can acquire the tone of established fact. Human analysts therefore need both the time and the authority to question what automated systems produce rather than simply validate it. That also means protecting the collection capabilities that AI cannot replace. As open-source material becomes more abundant, the value of what cannot be found online rises. Human sources, financial intelligence, law enforcement access and legal process take years to cultivate and moments to lose. A budget cycle that trims them in favor of subscriptions is trading durable capability for a license that expires. The objective should not be to remove automation from intelligence work, but to ensure that automation remains subordinate to collection, verification and human judgment.

What Open Sources Cannot Close

I learned the limits of open-source work firsthand while researching foreign components in Russian strike drones. Open sources got me a long way. Recovered wreckage data, teardown imagery, part markings, and manufacturer documentation could establish what was inside these systems and who made it. That is valuable, and it was achievable by skilled analysts working in public.

But the questions that mattered most were different. Who actually bought a given part? Through which intermediaries did it move? Who paid for it, and through which accounts? Those gaps could not be closed by any amount of scraping. They required the tools that sit behind a legal threshold or inside a trusted relationship: law enforcement access to shipping and customs records, financial intelligence on transactions, and human sources with knowledge of how the networks operate. A dashboard could tell us a component existed. Only that other collection could tell us how it got there and who was responsible, which is the information policymakers need if they want to disrupt the supply chain rather than simply describe it.

That experience shaped how I think about the current issue. Open sources and closed collection are not competitors. The first made the second more efficient, because it let investigators ask better questions. The second made the first more meaningful, because it turned an interesting observation into an attributable finding. Treating either as a substitute for the other would have left us with a weaker product.

Defending the Analytical Craft

None of this is an argument against open-source intelligence. It is an argument for it, properly understood.

The practitioners who built the field's reputation, whether in newsrooms, nonprofits, academia, or government, are rigorous precisely because they distrust easy answers. They document their methods, show their chains of evidence, and say so when something can't be confirmed. That culture is the real asset. It is also what the commercial market is most at risk of undermining, because rigor is slow and expensive to sell, while a dashboard can be demoed in ten minutes.

The test I would offer any buyer, policymaker, or analyst is simple. When you are shown a claim, ask where it began, who else has independent knowledge of it, and what other collection could confirm or contradict it. If the system in front of you cannot answer those questions, it hasn't given you intelligence. It has given you a well-organized rumor.

The volume of open information will keep growing, and the tools to process it will keep improving. The scarce resource will not be data. It will be judgment, along with the access and tradecraft that make judgment possible. Agencies and firms that remember that, and invest accordingly, will see more clearly than those who confuse a full screen with a full picture.

item.title: Plurality of active-duty service members oppose Iran war: poll
item.description:
A plurality of active-duty service members oppose the military being used in the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, according to a poll conducted by Change Research for the advocacy group Common Defense

The poll surveyed 156 people currently serving in the military, 431 veterans, and 144 immediate family members of active-duty service members between September 15 and 28.

Common Defense is a veteran-led group that advocates for progressive policies and endorses Democratic candidates, though a 47% plurality of respondents to their September poll are self-identified Republicans. Nearly 20% identified as “pure independents,” while 35% said they were Democrats.

Though Republicans surveyed backed Operation Epic Fury at a rate of 77% to 16%, overwhelming opposition among Democrats and independents left respondents opposed to the war overall, 49% to 44%. Veterans were by far the most supportive of the ongoing conflict, with 53% in support and 44% opposing, while active-duty service members opposed it by a 16-point margin and military families by 38 points.

During a CBS News town hall that aired over the weekend, Vice President JD Vance faced questions from the grieving husband of Nicole Amor, one of six U.S. soldiers killed in an Iranian strike on a military base in Kuwait during the war’s opening days, about the “fundamental failures” that led to her death.

“There's a failure in leadership. And I want to know how this administration is gonna start holding those leaders accountable for the actions and the deaths of the soldiers that we honor and that we love,” Joey Amor told Vance.

The vice president responded that it was “literally the first time” he’d heard of these failures and pledged to “figure out what exactly happened and what exactly we can do better."

In the Common Defense poll, 55% of those surveyed named “the length of deployments and troops' health, safety, and welfare during the war with Iran” as one of the top issues Congress should investigate — the second-most commonly given answer, following Chinese access to the U.S. supply chain.

Besides the Iran war, a plurality of respondents opposed using the military for domestic policing and for assisting Israel’s military in regional wars. Overall, respondents opposed the U.S. military being deployed to assist Israel’s military aims in Gaza and Lebanon” by 53%-38%. A majority of respondents supported the use of the military for strikes on drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and for border deployments.

Some of the more explicitly political questions, including approval ratings for President Donald Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, were fairly split, but almost 80% of respondents agreed that “veterans and military families are being left behind by politicians and society.” A mere 15% disagreed.

"For too long, politicians have used veterans as a backdrop for their speeches instead of listening to what we actually have to say," Naveed Shah, U.S. Army veteran and the political director at Common Defense, said in a statement. "Even in a sample that leans older, whiter, and more conservative than the country, two-thirds of military voters say the decisions affecting our troops are about politics, not readiness.”

Recent polling has shown that among the general public, the war in Iran is among voters’ top concerns as midterms approach.

item.title: How the UAE and MEK weaponize AI to spread propaganda
item.description:
Somewhere inside Iran, a network of activists exchanged messages about politics and news with an activist — nicknamed “Parsa” — on the messaging app Telegram. They had no idea they were actually speaking to an AI agent that had copied the real activist’s style by training it on 8,400 real Telegram posts.

Instead of “Parsa,” they were actually communicating with the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK), an Iranian Islamist-Marxist opposition group widely regarded as a cult.

According to a report from Anthropic released last month, this operation was carried out by four individuals working for the MEK. They built an AI agent named “Viktor” that also surveilled individuals inside Iran and flooded social media platforms with pro-MEK content under “independent” branding.

The Anthropic report sheds light on how foreign actors are increasingly using artificial intelligence tools like Claude and ChatGPT for their influence operations. AI agents like Viktor are software systems powered by large-language models that can operate autonomously. A lot of the actions described in the report — like drafting reports, creating content, compiling information — looks like ordinary work similar to what millions of Americans use Claude and ChatGPT for.

Perhaps the report’s biggest surprise is the degree to which U.S.-aligned groups and partners have embraced AI for their influence operations.

The MEK, for example, boasts notable support on Capitol Hill. Last year, 230 members of the House co-sponsored a resolution urging U.S. support for the MEK’s plan for Iran. Former National Security Adviser John Bolton, former Vice President Mike Pence, and former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani are just a handful of high-profile Republican politicians who have spoken at MEK rallies, often for a hefty speaking fee.

One account managed by the MEK-linked “Viktor,” @Tehranchekhabar19, boasts over 170,000 followers on Instagram. The account presents itself as an independent news account while posting content that support the MEK’s views, such as videos that promote the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran while attacking Reza Pahlavi, the former Crown Prince of Iran who leads a rival opposition faction. The account’s videos sometimes garner hundreds of thousands of views. “Viktor” also set up other Instagram accounts boasting hundreds of thousands of followers, some of which appear to have since been shut down.

The MEK, which the U.S. listed as a Foreign Terrorist Organization until 2012, was even more active on Telegram to try to covertly recruit people inside Iran to support the MEK’s agenda. According to Anthropic, “Viktor” infiltrated more than 500 groups on Telegram, then “grouped these targets by city, age, occupation, political alignment, and arrest history likely to help them tailor their messages to the specific audiences.”

Craig Holman, Government Affairs Lobbyist for Public Citizen, explained in an email to RS that this marks a new type of influence tactic. “These accounts of foreign governments using AI to manipulate the opinions of legislative bodies and the public are based on the root source of AI deception: falsely depicting a real person or entity doing or saying something that they never did.”

This case study and others described in similar reports reveal that foreign actors are taking concrete steps to add AI to their arsenal of weapons to win information wars. For instance, a report from OpenAI published last week detailed how Iranian operators successfully placed almost 100 articles in different international affairs-focused publications under phony bylines using ChatGPT. The Iran-written articles typically promoted an anti-Iran War point of view, with headlines such as “Is America’s Iran Policy Being Privatized? The Jared Kushner Question” and “Trump’s Iran Gamble Hardened the Regime It Meant to Break.”

The recent OpenAI report also found that Russia had successfully created and controlled a fake think tank called the “Social Research Center” with real staff on the ground in Latin America who had no idea they were working for Russia. Russian operators used ChatGPT to create content and draft internal reports. Meanwhile the unknowing staff carried out real interviews with experts and published research papers, mostly about India-Latin America relations.

While the Social Research Center’s X account has been suspended, the organization’s website is still active as of publication. There, it posted a statement rejecting OpenAI’s claims as “factually incorrect and as constituting a deliberate attempt to discredit an independent research project.”

Another case study revealed how one of Washington’s closest partners in the Middle East is embracing AI to absolve itself of its role in a bloody civil war.

The UAE’s “Deadshot”


Emirati officials created their own AI agent on Claude, nicknamed “Deadshot” — and charged it with the herculean task of whitewashing the UAE’s role in the Sudanese civil war. A UAE-backed Sudanese paramilitary group, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has been credibly accused of ethnic cleansing and sexual violence. A U.N. fact-finding mission had said that the RSF’s actions against non-Arab communities in Sudan’s Darfur region bear the “hallmarks of genocide.”

The AI agent got right to work to maintain the UAE’s reputation, targeting the U.N. in particular. According to the Anthropic report, “Deadshot” hijacked the identity of a real Sudanese human rights organization and ghost-wrote U.N. testimony in hopes that the world body would be influenced by “independent local witnesses, rather than state messaging.”

Anthropic’s report gives conflicting accounts as to whether the effort was successful. At one point, it says it could not confirm whether the testimony reached its intended audience, though a summary elsewhere in the report describes it as having been “delivered in a live UN Human Rights Council session.” Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.

Deadshot compiled information on the UAE’s critics, creating “counter-accountability dossiers” on U.N. Special Rapporteurs who had criticized the UAE’s role in Sudan.

The UAE also carried out a broader information campaign centered primarily on X. “Deadshot” created and managed a network of around 300 inauthentic social media accounts that posted content to pin the blame for the Sudanese civil war on the Muslim Brotherhood, which is supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces against the RSF.

The posts themselves often make humanitarian appeals, deflecting blame for the war away from the RSF and toward the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood, which the U.S. designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization earlier this year. “The longer Sudan’s war drags on, the deeper the famine crisis becomes. Analysts point to hardline Islamist elements supporting continued military confrontation over negotiated settlements,” reads one post on X by a user with 27,000 followers that Anthropic says was part of the coordinated campaign. Another post on X from a user with 119,000 followers says the SMB role in the conflict “makes ending the war far harder.”

According to the report, the operator instructed Claude to carry out a “coordinated transatlantic and regional operation to dismantle the Muslim Brotherhood globally” hundreds of times.

Kholood Khair, Founding Director of Khartoum-based think tank Confluence Advisory, explained in an interview with RS that the Sudanese conflict is being fought on three fronts: the battlefield, the mediation table, and the information space — and that last one is becoming more crucial. “These posts are carefully deployed to attempt to co-opt the pro-civilian rule, pro-democracy movement and camouflage what the UAE is actually trying to achieve in Sudan,” said Khair. She noted that, while many of the posts aren’t factually incorrect, they are selective in the narrative they tell.

“AI is the next battleground in many of these wars, and Sudan’s war has clearly become a testing ground, with the UAE getting a head start, ” Khair added.

item.title: As Houthis encircle Taiz, Yemen's Saudi-backed gov't faces disaster
item.description:
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, endured a siege from 2015 to 2017. Today, it is encircled again.

The World Food Program says it cannot reach more than 600,000 people in and around the city. The International Organization for Migration counts over 200,000 people displaced since the Houthi offensive on Yemen’s Red Sea coast launched in September.

Why this city, and why now? The Houthis, formally known as the Ansar Allah movement, draw their strength from the Zaydi Shia highlands of the north. Critics say their governing ideology rests on the belief that the right to rule belongs to sayyids, descendants of the Prophet Mohammad, a lineage to which the Houthi family itself belongs. The Houthis have long denied seeking to restore the Imamate, but in Taiz, which has for a decade resisted Houthi encroachment, that denial finds few believers.

Taiz has a long history of political activism and hostility to the idea of religious hereditary rule. Its poets and journalists supplied much of the dissident energy that toppled the Imamate in 1962, and its streets were one of the centers of the 2011 uprising against then-President Ali Abdallah Saleh. This gives the governorate symbolic weight disproportionate to its size.

Moreover, Taiz is significant for its geography. It sits at the hinge between the Red Sea coast and the southern highlands that shelter the city of Aden, currently the administrative capital of Yemen’s internationally-recognized government, which the Houthis struck last week with missiles. Houthi control of the surrounding mountains would make the government’s counteroffensive around the Bab al-Mandab strait far harder to sustain.

That counteroffensive, known as Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” was announced on October 5 by President Rashad al-Alimi, a native of the Taiz governorate who chairs the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, the body that leads Yemen’s internationally-recognized government.

The stated aim of the counteroffensive is to recover the whole country from the Houthis, the capital Sana’a included. So far, it seems to have stalled in its second week.

Government forces, under heavy Saudi air cover, have retaken ground around Bab al-Mandab and Dhubab. But Mokha, the coastal prize the Houthis seized in September, remains in Houthi hands.

The Houthis hold a contiguous area and can shift forces and materiel between fronts with relative ease. Their opponents consist of numerous factions fighting under the government umbrella, each of which answers to different commanders with different political projects. When the west coast collapsed in September, Tareq Saleh, who heads the National Resistance Forces that held the coast, withdrew to Aden, where southern units initially refused his men entry. The southerners' wariness stems from the role Saleh's uncle, then president, played in the 1994 civil war, when northern forces overran the south and crushed their bid for independence.

Indeed, Yemen’s civil war was already heavily shaped by external forces. Today, it has grown even more tightly bound to the wider U.S.- Iran war.

Since July, the Houthis have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping and turned their arsenal on the kingdom itself. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been attacked multiple times this month, with 13 killed and over 300 wounded.

The Houthis also hit Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran last week, with fire spreading across several floors. Reuters estimates Saudi crude output ran below 7 million barrels a day for most of the first six months of the U.S.-Iran war, leading to $50 billion in lost revenue at current prices. The International Monetary Fund expects the Saudi economy to shrink by 3.3% this year.

Riyadh’s response has been aggressive in substance toward the Houthis but restrained in tone toward Iran, the movement's primary patron. Saudi Arabia says it has carried out waves of air and missile strikes on Houthi territory, yet Saudi officials largely stop short of naming Tehran.

The reticence is probably deliberate. Riyadh has every reason to preserve room for a deal between Washington and Tehran that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and hopefully end attacks from Iran and Iran-aligned groups on Saudi soil. Iran is also the outside power with the most influence over the Houthis. If Tehran chose to press them to de-escalate, that could create space for a Saudi-Houthi ceasefire and talks.

In the meantime, the kingdom has few viable options to escalate pressure on the Houthis, who set the tempo of escalation.

Turkey and Pakistan have activated the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, but both describe their roles as defensive. Egypt’s President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi on Saturday asked parliament for authority to militarily support the kingdom, but stressed that “we are speaking only about defense.”

President Donald Trump recently noted that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and suggested he may ask Turkey to get more involved. Yet, with midterm elections looming on November 3, a war on Iran that has dragged on for eight months without settlement, and oil prices climbing, another American campaign in Yemen is the last thing the White House wants.

Riyadh, short of options, has yet to offer a comprehensive strategy beyond punitive airstrikes on the Houthis and support for its Yemeni partners’ counteroffensive, which is faring poorly, as the siege of Taiz makes clear.

The best clue to official thinking is a recent column by Abdulrahman al-Rashed, a former editor of Asharq al-Awsat and a well-connected Saudi commentator. He answers those who argue that the world should simply negotiate with the Houthis, as it has with other rulers of Sana’a.

The Houthi project, he argues, “is fundamentally at odds with the very idea of the state.” He describes how the Houthis have used all concessions and pauses to re-arm and wage war, calling the group “yet another Iranian proxy in the region, not the nucleus of an ordinary Yemeni system of government.”

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman appears to share this view that the Houthis are not a group to be accommodated. Chairing the cabinet on October 13, he declared that the “terrorist Houthi militia will face the consequences of its heinous crimes and attacks.”

Tehran’s position, meanwhile, has been contradictory. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei says Iran will help mediate if both sides ask and denies any role in Yemeni operations. Yet numerous investigative reports demonstrate that Iranian advisers and intelligence actively enabled the Houthi capture of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

Though Saudi Arabia has not responded to the mediation offer, the foreign minister of Yemen’s internationally-recognized government, Afrah al-Zouba, rejected it, calling Iran a “party to the war against the Yemeni people.”

This is not a surprising response. Iran’s own hardline press betrays official neutrality, running headlines that celebrate Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities.

One report in Kayhan, whose editor-in-chief is selected by Iran's supreme leader, refers to the Houthis as the “Yemeni resistance” and frames war in Yemen as a “twelve-year aggression of the Saudi-American coalition.” Moreover, an adviser to the parliamentary speaker, one of the key negotiators with the U.S., wrote that Iran would use “tools in the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb and beyond” to keep oil prices elevated.

More telling is the extent to which Tehran has adopted the Houthi vocabulary. Iranian officials describe the Houthis as “Yemen’s armed forces,” overlooking the Saudi-backed government that holds Yemen’s U.N. seat, and call Saudi restrictions on flights and ports in Houthi-held territory a “blockade.” Riyadh sees those measures as the enforcement of a U.N.-backed arms embargo and as support for Yemen’s recognized government, whose current executive council took shape under Saudi sponsorship in 2022, after Riyadh pressed the previous president to step aside and transfer his powers to the newly created governing council.

Iran thus arrives with its position on the central questions already fixed, rendering its mediation offers largely hollow. Any Saudi move to the table would look like a concession to the Houthis’ and Tehran’s framing. That makes talks harder for Riyadh, even if it wanted them.

item.title: What happened to all the concern about Venezuelan democracy?
item.description:
The rise of right-wing governments in Latin America has reshaped the region's political landscape. As a new wave of conservative leaders takes office, the region is moving closer to Washington to a degree not seen in decades. Nowhere is this shift more evident than in the changing political approach to Venezuela.

Just a year ago, governments across the region were condemning Nicolás Maduro's authoritarianism, questioning the legitimacy of his electoral victories and supporting international pressure on Caracas. Today, many engage directly with Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro's former vice president and Venezuela's interim president. The region has moved from demanding democratic change in Caracas to normalizing relations with the very political establishment it once sought to isolate.

Looking back at the previous decade makes this contrast clearer. With few exceptions, Latin America had adopted an increasingly firm stance against Maduro's authoritarian rule. In 2017, after Maduro stripped the opposition-controlled National Assembly of its powers, the founding members of the Southern Common Market, or Mercosur, suspended Venezuela indefinitely under the democracy provisions of the Ushuaia Protocol.

A few days later, a coalition of mostly center-right governments, including Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Paraguay and Peru, established the Lima Group to coordinate pressure on Caracas. In 2018, five of its members joined Canada in referring the situation in Venezuela to the International Criminal Court. The group rejected Maduro's reelection the same year, later supported Juan Guaidó's claim to the interim presidency, and pressed for sanctions. By 2019, Maduro had become largely isolated in his own region.

Venezuela's neighbors adopted a similar position after the 2024 election. The National Electoral Council declared Maduro the winner without publishing polling station-level results, while opposition tallies showed Edmundo González winning by a substantial margin. Governments across the political spectrum, from Gabriel Boric's left-wing Chile to Javier Milei's right-wing Argentina, rejected the official outcome. Maduro's government expelled diplomats from several countries in response. Caracas severed diplomatic relations after President Santiago Peña recognized González as the president-elect.

These political efforts undermined Maduro’s international legitimacy and signaled that Venezuela's crisis was not merely an internal matter. This isolation helped shape the political context for the U.S. military operation that resulted in Maduro's capture on Jan. 3.

Following Washington's lead


The events that followed Maduro's capture caught the region's right-wing governments off guard. Instead of bringing González and his political ally María Corina Machado to power, the Trump administration chose to work with Rodríguez, one of the regime's leading figures. Rodríguez continues to govern with Washington's backing.

This decision left the region's right-wing governments in a difficult position. For years, they had argued that the regime in Venezuela lacked democratic legitimacy. Yet when Washington chose to replace its leader without dismantling the regime, these governments remained largely silent. As the Trump administration deepened its relationship with Rodríguez, most of the region followed suit.

Now, leaders who placed democratic legitimacy at the center of their foreign policies are now cooperating with a different face of the same Chavista system.

Paraguay is one of the clearest examples. Peña lost diplomatic relations with Caracas after recognizing González as the winner of the 2024 election. Yet on Sept. 19, he became the second foreign head of state to visit Venezuela since Maduro's removal. As Julieta Heduvan, a Paraguayan foreign policy analyst, argued, the gesture toward Venezuela "must be read in light of Asunción's realignment with Washington." The result, she concluded, is "a foreign policy that sacrifices doctrinal coherence without obtaining in return either bilateral progress or democratic guarantees."

Chile's president, José Antonio Kast, has followed a similar path. In December 2025, as president-elect, he called for an end to Venezuela's dictatorship, and he later welcomed the U.S. operation against Maduro. Yet on Sept. 23, one day after Trump met with Rodríguez, Kast sat down with her at the U.N. to discuss restoring bilateral relations.

The Dominican Republic offers yet another example of this emerging trend. In 2024, Caracas expelled Dominican diplomats and suspended flights between the two countries after President Luis Abinader joined governments questioning Maduro's reelection. This month, Abinader met Rodríguez on the sidelines of the World Food Forum in Rome, where they discussed Dominican purchases of Venezuelan fuel and gas.

It is no coincidence that Paraguay, Chile and the Dominican Republic all belong to the Shield of the Americas, the security coalition Trump launched in March, which Christopher Sabatini of Chatham House called a "Trumpista-only" alliance. Frank Mora, a former U.S. ambassador to the Organization of American States, told me that Paraguay, Chile and other right-wing governments are adjusting their Venezuela approach to align with Washington. Visiting Caracas, sitting down with Rodríguez and improving relations is a proactive way to win Washington's favor. Rather than risk repercussions by pressing for more democracy in Venezuela, they line up behind the U.S. position and make that alignment visible.

Practical concerns, including migration, trade and consular services, also play a role. Caracas has reestablished consular relations with Chile, Ecuador, Peru and the Dominican Republic. These governments are under domestic pressure to send Venezuelan migrants home, as voters across the region increasingly blame them for rising crime. In Chile, for example, Kast campaigned on linking immigration to organized crime and has pledged to expel more than 300,000 undocumented migrants, which will require diplomatic relations with Venezuela.

These states also have a clear economic incentive. With Washington’s recent engagement in Venezuela, Mora said there is a "gold rush," and these governments are creating a political space for their investors to share in the benefits.

The region's principled stance that guided its policy toward Venezuela before Jan. 3 has largely evaporated. As Venezuelan analyst Andrés Cañizález put it, "what was once handled through bombastic declarations, diplomatic ruptures, and multilateral pressure has turned into a pragmatism that prioritizes rebuilding bilateral ties, managing migration flows, and economic cooperation, always within the boundaries set by Washington."

As countries across the region deepen their ties with this new version of Chavismo, remarkably little has changed in Venezuela to justify the rapprochement. Diosdado Cabello, a longtime Chavista figure associated with years of human rights abuses, remains interior minister. Rodríguez's brother, Jorge, heads the National Assembly. The new defense minister previously led the intelligence service and has been sanctioned by the United States, Canada and the European Union over repression under his command.

The human rights group Foro Penal still counted 344 political prisoners in September, and there is still no established timetable for elections. Ten months after the U.S. operation to capture Maduro, the main obstacle to democratization is now the political and institutional system that has survived him.

The cost of selective democracy


What makes this shift even more ironic is that the governments now getting closer to Rodríguez spent years criticizing Brazil and Mexico for failing to exert sufficient pressure on Maduro. They accused those countries of enabling authoritarianism because they refused to join the Lima Group or support sanctions.

Today, those critics are doing the same, and not because Venezuela has become any more democratic. The decisive factor is Washington’s change of course. For many governments in Latin America, democratic principles and electoral legitimacy are becoming secondary considerations, defended mostly when they align with Washington’s preferences.

Yet a democratic and prosperous Venezuela is in the interests of both Latin America and the United States. Diplomatic engagement with Caracas can be used to demand political reforms, press for the release of political prisoners and secure a credible timetable for elections. Rodríguez’s pledge at the United Nations that Venezuela would hold elections, and the U.S.-backed negotiations now underway, give regional governments an opening to secure concrete commitments.

Latin American countries do not have to choose between aligning themselves with Washington and losing their voice. The region can regain its influence as an independent political actor in shaping Venezuela’s future. But doing so will require more than restoring diplomatic ties; it will require using these ties to achieve tangible progress toward democratization.

item.title: Trump might respond to Zelensky’s stance with campaign of maximum pressure — expert
A new 'Danube' approach to the Hormuz Strait is in order
item.description:
During the ongoing conflict between Iran and the United States, the Arab Gulf states have borne the brunt of Iranian drone and missile strikes while incurring mounting economic costs.

With limited prospects for a U.S.-Iran settlement, Gulf states, using Oman as an interlocutor, have pursued talks with Iran aimed at ending the conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. This reflects a significant shift in regional dynamics: Gulf states are increasingly exploring arrangements with Iran to restore navigation without direct U.S. involvement.

Even without U.S. acquiescence, securing a negotiated agreement will be difficult. Distrust between the Arab Gulf states and Iran runs deep, rooted in historic grievances and long-term contestation for hegemony in the Middle East. The ongoing conflict has intensified hostility and resentment on both sides.

But the conflict has also revealed the Gulf states’ vulnerability while underscoring the limits of the U.S. security umbrella. Recent Houthi and Iran-backed Iraqi militia attacks on Bab Al-Mandab and Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline highlight the limits of promoting alternative shipping routes and efforts by Arab Gulf states to engineer their way out of the crisis. The need for a resolution is increasingly urgent.

A return to the status quo ante, including a return to free transit under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), seems increasingly unlikely. Replacing the norms of international maritime law with a regime allowing Iran to impose tariffs, which seems to be the basis for discussions between Oman and Iran, is untenable. While transit fees might be part of the long-term resolution, Arab Gulf states will reject any arrangement that suggests Iranian sovereignty over the strait. In fact, such an approach might prolong security tensions, with the United States feeling bound to counter Iranian claims of control with strikes or at least regular freedom of navigation operations (FONOPs) through the strait.

History offers examples of alternative approaches to maintaining trade in the context of great-power competition. The most frequently cited precedent in this regard is the 1936 Montreux Convention, which continues to govern transit through Turkey’s Bosphorus and Dardanelles. The convention offers useful lessons for Hormuz, particularly in its approach to foreign naval access. But a more applicable model may come from a less obvious place: the Danube River after the Crimean War.

The 1856 Treaty of Paris established the European Commission of the Danube amid intense regional competition in Europe. Unable to secure an agreement on the use of the river, the signatories devised an approach that handed responsibility for navigability and shipping safety on the lower Danube to an independent international organization.

While the signatories maintained oversight through a board, the commission operated independently, even charging tolls and raising debt to fund trade infrastructure expansion. By delegating management of the river to an independent body, competing powers reduced potential flashpoints while allowing all of Europe to benefit from trade along the Danube, which runs from what is now southwestern Germany to the Black Sea coast between modern Romania and Ukraine. Initially seen as a temporary expedient, the commission remained in place for over 85 years.

A similar Strait of Hormuz Commission could help return stability and trade flows to the region. The institution could be overseen by a board representing the eight countries bordering the Gulf. Major trading partners in Asia and Europe, together with the United States, could participate through an advisory body, giving them influence and incentives to cooperate with the scheme without giving them a veto.

Initially, the commission would have a narrow mandate: ensuring safe commercial passage; coordinating escort, rescue, and environmental-response services; and maintaining facilities required for these functions. To reduce the risk of military miscalculation, the commission could require naval vessels to report intended transit and share that information with member states, as required under Montreux. Its costs could be covered by reasonable service charges, tolls or member financing.

The Danube approach would allow the institutional structure and responsibilities of the commission to develop incrementally. An initial agreement could establish principles and procedures for commercial transit, maritime safety and communication among the parties. More sensitive functions, from military deconfliction of the strait to support for broader regional infrastructure development, could be added as confidence in the commission develops.

The governing principle would be shared management without shared sovereignty. Neither Iran nor Oman would relinquish territorial claims, and the commission would acquire no sovereignty over the strait. Its authority would extend only to the management and security of navigation through the strait. The objective would not be to resolve the region’s rivalries, but to insulate one vital shared interest from them.

Crucially, establishing such a commission would not have to await a comprehensive settlement of the Gulf’s wider conflicts. Indeed, that would defeat much of its purpose. Concentrating on the narrower shared interest of restoring predictable commercial transit would give the countries of the region a platform for practical collaboration and building confidence. If successful, the commission would provide a foundation for constructive dialogue on more contentious issues, including Iran’s nuclear program, eliminating political interference and support for proxy groups, and resolving longstanding territorial disputes. The commission would not have a mandate to resolve these disputes, but it could help build trust and the habits of cooperation needed to address them through other diplomatic channels.

Critics will argue that negotiating such an arrangement rewards Iran for challenging international maritime law and using its geographical position to extract concessions. Others will voice concern about the precedent for strategic waterways such as the Strait of Malacca and Bab Al-Mandab.

Both concerns are legitimate. But insisting on a legal regime that can no longer reliably secure transit does not in itself reopen Hormuz. Nor would shared management of the strait require abandoning the principles of freedom of navigation. Ultimately, as the international rules-based order comes under growing pressure, upholding universal principles like freedom of navigation may require new arrangements that address local contexts and create incentives for neighboring states — including rivals — to uphold them.

For Iran and the Gulf states, the choice is ultimately pragmatic. Cooperation after years of distrust and the imposition of more recent wounds inflicted by the current conflict will be difficult. But a jointly established commission could reopen the strait for sustained trade while helping to address the parties’ core security and economic concerns.

More important, it would establish a model for the Gulf’s emerging security order: regionally-owned, internationally-supported, and built around the institutional management of shared interests rather than dependence on any single outside power.

item.title: Evidence of a Russian 'hybrid war' in Europe is vanishingly thin
item.description:
These days, barely a week goes by in Europe without a drone sighting, a fire or a power outage being blamed on Russia. We’re told that these incidents are all part of a relentless, and escalating, “hybrid war” that Moscow is waging against the continent.

Tensions escalated dramatically last month after Germany formally attributed to Moscow a “failed” drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport. But does the evidence support Western claims that Russia is engaged in a systematic hybrid war against Europe?

Various datasets and reports are regularly cited as evidence, including from Leiden University, the Soufan Center, the Associated Press and defense-related think tanks like the IISS, CSIS and GLOBSEC. Taken individually, each paints a bleak picture. Read side by side, however, they tell a very different story. For starters, the numbers don’t add up: depending on the report, Russia has launched between 52 and 255 hybrid attacks in Europe since February 2022, a fivefold discrepancy for what is supposed to be the same campaign.

The reason is that there is no agreed-upon definition of what a hybrid attack even is. The IISS itself admits that the term is “amorphous.” Some reports only count acts of physical sabotage; others include pro-Kremlin stickers, graffiti, peace demonstrations and even the Russian Navy passing through the English Channel. In other words, it is a concept that can be used to include almost anything. Moreover, in most cases, the evidence linking Russia is very weak or, in fact, non-existent. Evidence of Russian responsibility usually consists of news articles reporting that Western officials suspect so. If a government claims “Russia did it,” the case ends up on the list.

Yet many of the most widely publicised cases of alleged Russian sabotage — the “jamming” of the GPS signal of von der Leyen’s plane, the Baltic cable incidents in late 2024, a crashed DHL cargo plane, a fire at Heathrow Airport in 2025 — ended up collapsing upon basic scrutiny. In each case, Russian involvement was ultimately ruled out. The signal of von der Leyen’s plane, it turned out, was never lost. The Baltic cables were damaged by anchors dragged by Chinese- and Hong Kong-flagged ships, with investigators finding no evidence of intent. The DHL crash in Vilnius was caused by pilot error, and the Heathrow fire by a fault in a substation that had been identified years earlier but never fixed.But how many people actually know this, considering that such retractions generally receive a fraction of the coverage of the original allegations?

The same goes for the drone panic that swept Europe in the fall of 2025, when near-daily sightings caused the closure of several airports across the continent. Leaders openly blamed Moscow, yet virtually all the “Russian drone” sightings turned out to be unfounded: a Dutch investigation of some 60 incidents found “much panic and hardly any evidence of Russian involvement,” with many sightings turning out to be hobby drones, planes, helicopters, satellites or even stars.

Where Russian drones have indeed entered NATO airspace — in Poland, Romania, Moldova and Lithuania — this has almost always occurred near the Ukrainian border, during attacks on Ukrainian targets. Even the Lithuanian president has stated that the latest such incident was likely caused by a drone that veered off course because of Ukrainian jamming. This appears much more like fallout from the war next door than a deliberate campaign of incursions. There was one incident where a Russian drone was shot down deep in Polish territory, but even in this case Western intelligence officials “privately” admitted that the Russian incursion was probably not intentional.

And then there’s the Leipzig/Halle case. Following Germany’s official accusation of Russian involvement, NATO’s Secretary General Mark Rutte was quick to declare that “the evidence is clear.” This may very well be true, but since no evidence has actually been made public, we simply have to take the German authorities’ word for it. As a German professor told EUobserver, the attribution “may be plausible, but there is evidently no proof.”

Ultimately, once all the speculative and unproven “incidents” are set aside, what remains are a handful of demonstrable sabotage cases that have led to convictions, from a warehouse arson in London to torched buses in Prague,an IKEA fire in Vilnius and some GPS-tracker parcels sent toward Ukraine, allegedly to scout targets and transport routes for sabotage. Even in these cases, however, the courts have convicted low-level recruits, often contacted by anonymous handles on Telegram, and a connection to the Russian state or its proxies was established at a contested trial in only a handful of cases — notably the London warehouse fire and the GPS-tracker parcels in Germany — while elsewhere it rested on guilty pleas or closed hearings. But even assuming that Russia is indeed behind all these cases, the picture that emerges is one of few sporadic incidents with limited damage — hardly the “war” that European leaders routinely invoke.

So is this just a case of collective panic fuelled by click-addicted media? Or, given that the claims of a Russian “hybrid war” against Europe appear to rest on little more than propaganda, is there a concerted effort by the European Union-NATO establishment to condition citizens to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia?

The narrative clearly serves a variety of interests. For starters, it helps governments maintain support for an increasingly unpopular war in Ukraine and for a continental rearmament campaign that will require painful cuts to spending on other sectors. As a report by the Latvian Institute of International Affairs put it, the “nebulous tagline” of hybrid warfare would appear to be driven “by the need to goose flagging defense budgets and waning NATO cohesion.” It has worked: the drone panic has led to increased counter-drone spending at both the EU and NATO levels. Meanwhile, intelligence services have invoked the threat of sabotage to gain broader powers.

The specter of “Russian interference” also offers a broader authoritarian dividend, justifying everything from online censorship to the repression of dissent to election management — most egregiously in Romania, where an entire election was annulled because of an alleged Russian disinformation campaign for which no evidence of Russian involvement was ever provided. More recently, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, amid a push for greater EU ties, said it was “clear” that Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, without providing any evidence, even though several investigations have found little or no evidence to support this claim.

One may conclude that, to the extent that a “hybrid war” is being waged against Europe, it is being waged by the EU-NATO establishment itself against its own population, in the form of a prolonged campaign of psychological warfare aimed at inflating the Russian threat.

What is most concerning is the risk that this becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. NATO countries continue to enable — through intelligence, satellite and targeting support — Ukrainian deep strikes on Russia, including on civilian infrastructure, and each attack makes Russian retaliation against NATO territory more likely. If and when such an attack comes, it would be framed as an unprovoked escalation of Russia’s ongoing “hybrid war,” leaving little room for European restraint.

This is a classic security dilemma. In such a climate, it would take very little for a “hybrid war” that so far largely exists only on paper to rapidly evolve into a hot war between nuclear-armed powers.

In Italy, the expression “strategy of tension” evokes a dark period, from the late 60s to the early 80s, in which intelligence services and secret paramilitary networks operating under NATO auspices inflated the terrorist threat to frighten the electorate, including by engaging in terrorist acts that in some cases were then blamed on the left. European leaders should be wary of reviving such a strategy.

This article draws on an in-depth investigation published on the author’s Substack.

item.title: Europe’s dependence on America in space is hard to escape
America's Counter-Drone Authority Is Real, The Capacity Isn't Yet
item.description:
Here is a number worth sitting with: federal teams seized roughly 700 drones around World Cup venues this summer. Seven hundred — at one tournament, in one season, with the best-resourced counter-drone units in the world on the field. That figure is a success story and a warning in the same breath: the threat volume is enormous, and the federal government cannot be the only team suiting up for it.

Until this year, it legally had to be. The power to disable a hostile drone belonged to a short list of federal agencies, which left a state trooper at a stadium gate or a corrections captain watching an aircraft hover over his yard with nothing but binoculars and a report form. Congress ended that with the SAFER SKIES Act in December's defense bill, and the DHS-Justice framework implementing it has been in force since July 1: state, local, tribal, and territorial police and corrections agencies that complete federal training and certification, on approved equipment, can now track a threatening drone and — against a credible threat — take it out of the sky above major venues, critical infrastructure, and prisons.

And in the past week, Washington has shown it means to deliver. The Justice Department announced that the FBI's counter-drone training center in Huntsville will double its capacity. DHS's Science and Technology Directorate put commercial counter-drone systems through operational testing alongside state and local officers. The Pentagon selected four directed-energy systems for a homeland counter-drone pilot. This is what implementation momentum looks like, and the departments deserve real credit for it.

Now the hard truth: doubling a small number produces a small number. The Huntsville center's first class, last fall, held twelve officers, and it remains the only place in America where a state or local officer can earn the legal right to bring down a drone. More than 18,500 agencies are now eligible for these authorities. Against that denominator, even a doubled schoolhouse leaves the vast majority of American communities exactly where they were — watching — while the Super Bowl arrives in four months and the Los Angeles Olympics in under two years. Our prisons cannot wait either: drone incidents at federal correctional facilities rose twentyfold in six years, and state systems from South Carolina to Georgia are logging airborne contraband runs by the hundreds.

What turns momentum into coverage is money, sustained past the current news cycle. Congress should fund training at the scale of the authority it created: regional and satellite course delivery so a deputy in Phoenix is not waiting on a classroom seat in Alabama, instructor pipelines that multiply the schoolhouse instead of merely enlarging it, and a certification target tied to the event calendar that oversight committees actually track. Just as important, the FEMA counter-UAS grant program — $500 million across 2026 and 2027, built around the World Cup — should not sunset with the tournament that inspired it. The threat is not leaving when the fans do.

Governors have their own homework, and fewer excuses than ever: the grant rules push at least 97 percent of awarded funds down to local and tribal agencies within 45 days. The money is designed to reach the street. States should name a lead agency, compete for those dollars this cycle, and put their corrections systems and stadium districts first in line for certified teams.

Over more than twenty years in federal homeland security — the last of them leading U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement — I watched threats outrun statutes again and again. This time the statute arrived first, and this past week proved the executive branch intends to use it. The remaining question belongs to Congress and fifty governors: whether a nation that just confiscated 700 drones at a single sporting event will fund protection for everyone else. Authority without capacity is a promise. Appropriations are how promises get kept.
