Technology Is Outrunning the Way We Fight
item.description:
The United States is racing to field AI and autonomous systems. It is not racing to figure out how to fight with them. This imbalance between technology and concepts is widening a gap the U.S. is ill prepared to close. Ukraine has shown us why this gap is a threat: every new capability breeds a countermeasure, and technological advantage now spoils in months. The answer is not just faster innovation. It is making concept development a continuous military function, one that ties new technology to experimentation, validation, and adoption at the speed the fight demands. Not just a function of schoolhouses and Headquarters.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022 as a war of armored columns and maneuver. Today, trenches and minefields stretch for hundreds of miles, reminiscent of World War I; while drones, unmanned ground vehicles, precision munitions, and persistent surveillance hunt anything that moves.

The United States has poured considerable energy into buying and fielding new technologies faster, and has shown how we are endeavoring to learn from Ukraine. But the U.S. has put far less energy into the institutional processes we need to determine how we fight as technology and adversary behavior changes. This creates a consequential gap between what we build and how we fight.

This growing gap has two parts. The first is substance: technology and concepts need each other. A concept that ignores new technology will overlook new operational possibilities, while a new technology without a concept is a demonstration… not a warfighting capability.

The second is tempo: technology moves in weeks and months, while the processes that decide how formations should use it operate in years. Our fastest-ever concept cycle, from counterinsurgency doctrine to the Iraq Surge, took eighteen months. Most move slower still: gradual, methodical, and caked in decades of calcified bureaucracy.

The problem isn’t just that doctrine changes more slowly than technology. Units in combat adapt fast. The greater challenge is translating those adaptations into concepts that can be tested, refined, integrated into combined-arms operations, and adopted across the force.

That doesn’t mean rewriting concepts every time a new drone appears. It means recognizing when a change in technology (or in the enemy) breaks assumptions behind how we fight, then testing and spreading the fix before it goes stale.

Concept development must become a continuous military function, not a periodic publication. The winner won’t be the side that buys technology fastest, but the side that turns it into battlefield advantage before the enemy adapts. Today, the U.S. is not built to do that quickly.

Ukraine: Adaptation as Necessity

Ukraine illustrates the increasingly reciprocal nature of battlefield adaptation. To date, every advantage has invited an answer. Both sides have changed their technology and tactics again and again in response to each other, and neither has held an edge for long.

Consider the first-person-view (FPV) drone. Cheap, attritable, and easy to build, FPVs turned every squad into a precision strike force. Electronic jamming became its counterpoint. Fiber-optic drones, immune to jamming, then entered the field. Each move created new openings and new limits, and forced changes in both the technology and how it was used.

The operational consequences extend well beyond FPV drones. Persistent surveillance paired with cheap precision strike has changed where and how formations can move, mass, resupply, and survive. Concealment, dispersion, and deception matter more than ever. A unit that concentrates in a location, moves in the open, or runs a predictable supply route becomes a target.

This is the more consequential lesson from Ukraine: a technological innovation may initially improve the effectiveness of a particular weapon or unit, but its broader significance emerges when it changes the conditions under which formations operate. Then the enemy adapts, and the cycle starts again. And again.

In Ukraine, technological advantage is perishable. The hard part isn’t fielding new capabilities. It’s recognizing when they, or the enemy’s countermeasures, demand a different way of fighting.

The American Challenge: From Innovation to Institutional Learning

For the United States, Ukraine demonstrates why concept development cannot remain an episodic activity conducted in schoolhouses and periodically revisited. The lesson is not that Ukrainian solutions are universally applicable. It’s that new technology and countermeasures can break operational assumptions faster than our institutions are built to respond.

The United States cannot just replicate Ukraine’s approach. U.S. forces fight expeditionary campaigns, integrate across joint and coalition formations, and answer to policy, legal, and safety requirements that a nation like Ukraine, fighting for its survival and territorial integrity, does not. The goal is Ukraine’s capacity to adapt, built to American requirements.

Our gap isn’t a shortage of experiments or innovation offices; efforts like the Army’s “Transformation in Contact” are putting new capabilities into units and learning from them. Our gap is having a pathway from what one unit learns, to what the whole force learns. A concept that works in one brigade may fail against a different enemy, in different terrain, or at a higher echelon. And a successful experiment rarely changes training, force design, or acquisition on its own.

Autonomy has raised the stakes and made our pathway to institutional learning an even greater necessity. A software update, a retrained model, or a new way of employing a system can change how technology behaves, and can quietly invalidate the conditions under which it was tested and fielded.

That is the problem assured autonomy is meant to solve. Assured autonomy is justified confidence that an autonomous system will do what it is supposed to do. It must therefore account for the whole relationship: the technology, how it is employed, and the environment it operates in. Continuous, evidence-based assessments can tell commanders when a change requires fresh evaluation and where the boundaries of responsible use lie. Built into the adaptation process, assurance can support speed without abandoning safety, reliability, accountability, or established approval authorities.

Building an Adaptive Concept-Development Enterprise

The United States needs a repeatable process that links new technology, operational concepts, experimentation against a thinking enemy, validation, and adoption across the force.

We are suggesting neither a prototype nor a concept paper. It’s a validated, revisable concept of employment, backed by operational evidence: how a formation can fight differently, under what conditions that works, and what it takes to make it happen. Four functions are needed to get us there:

First, connect concept and technology development directly to operational formations.

Operators, technologists, testers, and concept developers should work alongside commanders. Their job goes beyond improving systems or inventing tactics: they should identify which operational assumptions a new capability breaks, and draft concepts to test.

Not every improvement demands a new concept. A better jammer may only need a new tactic; a capability that changes how a brigade moves, masses, or resupplies demands a new way of fighting. The force needs people close enough to the fight to tell the difference.

In Ukraine, operational units have designated innovation officers liaising directly with industry; industry partners provide prototypes, receive feedback on battlefield experimentation and adaptation. Through this relationship, operators, technologists, and testers converge on a specific requirement, and battalion-level Commanders have the authority to acquire the necessary prototypes to integrate into their formations.

Second, establish a persistent cycle of adversarial operational experimentation.

The question isn’t whether the technology works as designed. It’s whether the formation using it accomplishes the mission better against an opponent who adapts. Experiments should also find where a concept fails: what works against one threat may fail against another, and a promising system may impose unacceptable costs elsewhere in the formation.

Combat training centers, experimentation units, and operational formations already provide the foundation. The task is to link them into a persistent learning loop, fed by operational evidence and intelligence.

Ukraine offers a cautionary tale. For nearly three years, intelligence indicated Russia was developing jet-powered Shahed variants, by most accounts ample time to prepare countermeasures. But when Russia began launching these faster one-way attack systems, Ukraine had too few interceptors capable of that speed, and their previous interception tactics were insufficient to stop them. The warning did not sufficiently feed a cycle of experimentation before the threat was fielded. That gap cost lives.

Third, connect operational validation to adaptive fielding.

Today, a system is typically tested, approved, and fielded as a finished product. But in a fight like Ukraine’s, nothing stays finished: software is updated, models are retrained, and units find new ways to employ what they have. Each change can quietly invalidate the evidence behind the original fielding decision. Adaptive fielding treats validation as continuous, asking what has changed and whether the earlier evidence still holds.

For autonomous systems, this is where assured autonomy matters most, and where scrutiny should match the modification. A minor software patch for a drone flying the same mission in the same conditions may need only a quick check. Retraining its targeting model, sending it into a new environment, or reducing human supervision demands full re-evaluation. This doesn’t bypass approval authorities or testing requirements. It gives them a faster, evidence-based way to decide when more evaluation is needed.

Fourth, institutionalize validated concepts across the force.

This is the decisive step. Experimentation produces evidence; learning happens only when that evidence changes how the force trains, organizes, equips, and fights.

A counter-drone tactic proven in one division should appear in the next combat training center rotation, the next force design update, and the next acquisition…not in an after-action report on a shelf.

This change requires a defined pathway and clear authorities. Commanders, testers, capability developers, and acquisition officials each own different decisions, but those decisions must draw on a common body of operational evidence, with clear decision points for when the evidence is strong enough to act. The result is a continuous cycle: develop, experiment, validate, field, learn, institutionalize, adapt. Then repeat, as the technology and the enemy change.

In Ukraine, Aerorozvidka, a non-governmental organization, plays this role: not a think tank but an empowered change agent -- capturing evidence from the field and shepherding it through commanders, technologists, and acquisition officials until new tech is deployed or new concepts (like deep strike) are fielded.

Operational Advantage Depends on the Capacity to Learn

The United States possesses substantial technological, industrial, and innovative capacity to compete in AI and autonomous warfare. But technological leadership alone will not produce operational advantage. Adapting a system isn’t the same as adapting a force, and a better-performing unit doesn’t change the course of a campaign.

Four questions will dictate our capacity to learn: The technical question is what a system can do. The tactical question is how formations should employ it. The operational question is how it changes the way maneuver, fires, intelligence, protection, sustainment, and command combine to win. The strategic question is whether the institution can answer all three, again and again, faster than the enemy.

The race isn’t to build the best autonomous systems or to field them first. It’s to turn technological change into operational advantage, faster than the enemy can take it away. In the age of AI and autonomy, the force that learns fastest wins.

The Thirteenth Mile: This Is What Gray Zone War Looks Like
item.description:
On the morning of October 23, the cargo ship Khoryv sent a distress call 13 nautical miles off Constanța, Romania. Territorial waters end at twelve. Whoever flew the drone that sank her knew where the line was, and chose to stand one mile outside it.

That mile is the story. It is the difference between an attack on a NATO member and an incident in a NATO member's exclusive economic zone. It is the difference between Article 5 and a press release. The London insurance market understood this before most capitals did. When the Joint War Committee extended its Black Sea listed area on September 16, it covered the entire sea except the territorial waters of Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania and Turkey. The underwriters drew the same line the drone operators did. Nobody should find that comforting.

This is what gray zone conflict looks like. Freighters burning off the coasts of two NATO allies, sailors lost in cold water, and attacks clustered around the Sulina Channel, which became the main outlet for Ukrainian grain after Russia hammered Ukraine's own ports. It is war at a time and place of the attacker's choosing, priced just below the point where anyone is obliged to do anything about it.

"The problem is that we cannot prove it"

Bulgaria's prime minister, Rumen Radev, is nobody's idea of a Russia hawk. He told his parliament the logic of the attacks points to Moscow, and then said the quiet part out loud: "The problem is that we cannot prove it."

NATO's response has been built to solve Radev's problem. After the North Atlantic Council met on October 20, the Alliance announced it would send maritime patrol aircraft, radar, drones, intelligence personnel and forensic teams to examine the explosives. A U.S. Navy P-8 Poseidon is already flying the Black Sea. These are sensible deployments. They are also answers to the wrong question.

Play the scenario out. Grant NATO perfect attribution. The forensic teams recover a guidance board with Russian markings. The P-8 tracks a launch back to a known site. The Alliance announces, with high confidence, that the Russian Federation sank the ship. Now make it worse: the next drone hits a tanker alongside the pier at Constanța, the fire spreads, and thousands of civilians are dead.

The Kremlin denies it. Within the hour, Russian state media points at Kyiv, and it doesn't have to work hard to sell the story. Ukraine has been running its own maritime drone campaign since July, so the Black Sea is full of Ukrainian drones, and everyone knows it. A few Western commentators find the denial "plausible enough to warrant caution." Allies invoke Article 4 and consult. Statements are issued. Sanctions, already near their ceiling, are tightened at the margins. Then nothing happens, because every capital in the room is doing the same arithmetic: Russia has nuclear weapons, the Black Sea is not worth a war, and the dead are already dead.

You don't have to imagine that sequence. We ran it on July 17, 2014, when a Buk missile destroyed Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 over eastern Ukraine and killed everyone aboard. A Dutch-led investigation established in 2016 that the launcher had been delivered from Russia, and by 2018 that it came from a Russian army unit. The ICAO Council found Russia responsible in May 2025. The European Court of Human Rights did the same that July. Moscow denied all of it, spent years promoting theories that blamed Ukraine, and in 2022 invaded the country the missile had been fired over. Attribution was as good as attribution gets. The consequence, eleven years later, was an order to enter into good-faith negotiations on reparations.

That is the lesson Moscow took from MH17, and it is the one we refuse to learn. Deniability is not a shield for the attacker. It is a gift to the defender who would rather not act. Russia doesn't need us to believe its denials. It only needs us to want to.

Operational freedom is the target

The point of these strikes isn't the ships. It's the water around them. Every hull that burns off Sulina raises the premium on the next one, pushes a charterer toward a different route, and teaches a shipowner that a NATO coastline offers no protection. The attacker never has to declare a blockade. The market imposes it for him. Freedom of action shrinks by increments, each too small to justify a response, until the defender wakes up to find that the sea he was sure he controlled has a new landlord.

This is how Russia and China will impose costs on the West for the foreseeable future. Not with the decisive battle our doctrine, our budgets, and our military exercises are built around, but with a steady accumulation of incidents chosen for their deniability, timed to our distractions, and calibrated to our fear of escalation. Salami slicing is not a new idea; Beijing has practiced it in the South China Sea for more than a decade. What's new is the drone, which makes the slicing cheap, precise and anonymous.

The honest complication

The Black Sea gray zone is not one-sided, and pretending otherwise hands Moscow its talking points. Ukraine's Operation Molochka, launched in July, claims to have disabled 300 Russian-linked vessels in the Black and Azov Seas. Turkey's foreign minister says both sides are mounting heavy attacks to establish superiority before winter.

The distinction holds. Ukraine is striking the logistics of the country that invaded it, mostly sanctioned tankers serving Russian ports and occupied Crimea. Russia is striking grain ships in the economic zones of two NATO members that are not party to the war, with the apparent aim of making Ukraine's last reliable export route uninsurable. One is a belligerent waging war at sea. The other is exporting that war to the Alliance's doorstep and daring it to notice.

Taiwan won't look like Hellscape

If you want to know what a Taiwan conflict will look like, watch the Black Sea.

In 2024, Adm. Samuel Paparo said he wanted to "turn the Taiwan Strait into an unmanned hellscape" to defeat what he described as Beijing's likely plan: a massive attack with little warning. It's a sound concept, and the CNAS work that fleshed it out this year is serious. Hellscape is built to break an amphibious assault at the water's edge.

Beijing is rehearsing something else. The PLA's Justice Mission 2025 drills in December, run alongside the China Coast Guard, simulated a blockade of Taiwan's main ports and control of the waterways that carry its energy imports. This year the China Coast Guard and Maritime Safety Administration have run what the Jamestown Foundation calls a "quasi-quarantine" east of the island, creating the appearance of administrative control without declaring a blockade. Taiwan has already prosecuted a Chinese captain for severing an undersea cable. Each step is a law enforcement action, an inspection, an accident. None of them is an invasion.

A drone swarm waiting in the Strait for a landing force has nothing to shoot at when the adversary is a coast guard cutter boarding a container ship for a "safety inspection." The first Taiwanese or American drone to fire makes Taipei the aggressor. So Beijing won't cross the Strait. It will tighten the noose: a quarantine, a severed cable, an insurance listing, a shipping line that quietly decides Kaohsiung isn't worth the premium. It will bank on the world's risk aversion. It’s already working. After the May summit in Beijing, Washington paused a record $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, and the President described those sales as a "very good negotiating chip". Taiwan will not be conquered. It will be persuaded, one closed option at a time, that there is nothing left to defend.

Answering below the threshold

You cannot deter gray zone coercion with a capability designed for the war the adversary is careful never to start. The answer has to live in the same band the attacker does: below the threshold of general war, above the threshold of pain. Three steps would help in the Black Sea, and each has a Pacific twin.

Presence that denies, not presence that watches. Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria already run a Mine Countermeasures Task Group whose mandate was widened in July to cover undersea infrastructure. Montreux restricts warships of non-Black Sea states, not the littoral navies. Widen the mandate once more, to counter-drone escort of merchant traffic through allied economic zones, and buy the equipment from the Ukrainians who have kept their own grain corridor open under fire. In the Pacific, the equivalent is a convoy and escort plan for a quarantine, not only a kill chain for an invasion.

Decide the response before the incident. The moment of decision is where risk aversion wins, because it is always easier to wait for one more forensic report. Allies should agree in advance, and say publicly, what a verified strike on shipping in their waters will cost Moscow: a pre-approved tranche of capability released to Ukraine, a pre-agreed number of shadow fleet hulls detained. Attribution should trigger an equivalent consequence, not another discussion. Taipei and Washington need the same menu for a quarantine, written now, while no one is under pressure.

Take the market off the adversary's side. When insurers and charterers do the attacker's work, governments need a sovereign war-risk backstop for vessels trading to allied ports, so the next listed-area extension doesn't function as a blockade by spreadsheet. Taiwan will need that backstop on the first day of a quarantine, not the ninetieth.

None of this is escalation. It is the minimum required to make the gray zone cost something.

The Thirteenth Mile

The Khoryv went down one mile outside a line we drew. The adversary picked the mile. Next time it will pick the hour, the cargo, the flag and the ocean. The question for the Alliance isn't whether we can prove who did it. It's whether, once we prove it, we will do anything.

item.title: The Intelligence Community’s Missing Discipline
item.description:
Economic statecraft has become a primary instrument of US national security, deployed with a frequency and ambition that outpaces the intelligence architecture built to support it. For sanctions, tariffs, investment screening, export controls, and development finance to succeed, the United States must fully leverage the data and intelligence available to it. Now is the time for the IC to organize itself around the discipline of economic and financial intelligence.

The IC has long struggled to prove its value to economic customers: the Secretaries of Treasury, Commerce, Defense, and State, as well as the US Trade Representative and financial regulators. One frequent explanation is the IC’s historic orientation toward military and diplomatic support. Another is the perception that classified economic analysis lacks distinctive value. I spent most of a twenty-three-year intelligence career inside the economic discipline, ultimately leading Treasury’s Office of Intelligence and Analysis (OIA). While this may once have been true, the IC is doing better than ever to meet growing demand.

The problem is no longer the quality of the analysis—which has matured immensely—but the IC’s decentralized approach to serving its economic customers. No IC agency is specifically responsible for the discipline of economic and financial intelligence. The closest is OIA.

Congress created OIA in statute in 2004 with an eye toward sanctions support and countering terrorism finance. Its role has since expanded across economic, financial, and cyber issues for customers across government and industry. However, OIA is not the designated IC lead for US economic statecraft—no IC agency is. One consequence is that the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) remains the statutory lead for analytic support to the Treasury-led Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS). That made sense in 2007, when the Foreign Investment and National Security Act codified CFIUS and assigned the Director of National Intelligence that role. At the time, OIA was in its infancy and consumed by counterterrorism. That is no longer the case.

The instinct in Washington is to solve a challenge like this by first creating a new organization, then fixing the functions. Congress should start with the functions instead, then address where the discipline sits. To improve IC support to economic statecraft, Congress must first act on six fronts.

Designate a functional manager. One IC element must own economic and financial intelligence as a discipline: collection priorities, analytic standards, a hiring and training pipeline, and a framework for systematic engagement with allies and industry. Nothing about that role requires a new agency.

Clarify authorities. Explicitly authorize collaboration between the designated lead and both its government customers and the private sector, including exchange of expertise and data.

Supercharge private sector engagement. Many of the best national security solutions in economics and finance will come from industry. Create a permanent path for its ideas, expertise, and capabilities.

Work with what exists. Use OIA as the foundation and keep the number of IC agencies flat, but cap its size so it stays nimble as economic statecraft evolves.

Revisit ODNI’s CFIUS role. IC support to CFIUS sits with ODNI because in 2007 no one else could carry it. Whether it should move depends on where the discipline lands, but Congress should not view the 2007 answer as permanent.

Fund it as a national mission. Economic intelligence should not have to compete for a share of a domestic department’s topline. Give the discipline a dedicated budget line, with the investment in people and AI that exploiting economic data at scale requires.

That leaves where the discipline sits—and there are three answers, not one.

The easiest first step is a designation: name OIA the functional manager, leave it in Treasury, and make clear in statute and to policy customers that OIA is the center of gravity for economic and financial intelligence. That is available now and beats the status quo. Nevertheless, an IC office answering to the Secretary of the Treasury will always be seen—correctly—as Treasury’s first. This is why Commerce and others periodically press for shops of their own, an outcome that grows the IC rather than optimizing it.

The achievable reform is bureau status. Treasury did this with FinCEN in 2002, and FinCEN is now treated as a government-wide and international resource rather than Treasury’s alone. Done properly it means a separate appropriation, a director accountable to both the Secretary and the DNI, and a statutory mission naming service to the whole government, the private sector, and our allies.

The stretch option is to elevate OIA to become an independent National Geo-Economic Intelligence Agency—still my own preference, because only independence settles the question of whose intelligence office it is. But where the discipline sits is the last decision, not the first. Under any of the three, the proximity OIA has built with Treasury policymakers is a design problem with a known solution: dedicated, co-located teams at each major customer department.

Economic intelligence is a core national security capability and should be organized and resourced like one: purpose-built to track, anticipate, and disrupt adversary financial and commercial threats in real time. The playbook has changed. Our competitors are more agile, emboldened, and shaping markets and supply chains to their advantage while we debate whether the threat qualifies as strategic.

item.title: We’re Losing the Cognitive Space Race
item.description:
Over the last century, modern medicine achieved a historic feat. We increased the human lifespan by 33%. But at the same time, we completely failed to defend our brain healthspan. Today, a silent gap of 15 to 30 years exists between the time our bodies survive and the time our brains remain vibrant, innovative, and fully functional. It is a terrifying paradox. Medical science has advanced so much that a newborn today can realistically expect to live to 100, if not 120 years old. Yet, we passively accept that their cognitive engine will begin an irreversible, downhill slide in their thirties with the likelihood of dementia reaching almost 100% by the age of 110. What good is an extra three decades of biological existence if our brains lack the strength and resilience to enjoy it? This is no longer just a localized healthcare crisis; it is an imminent national security threat to our competitive edge.

Look at where our national focus and funding are directed. America is focused on investing billions of dollars into artificial intelligence and hypersonic defense systems. However, we are systematically ignoring the ultimate computing engine that builds the technology, commands our military, drives our economy, and stabilizes our communities: the human brain.

Our global competitors are not making this mistake. Most notably, China understands that future geopolitical dominance will not be won simply by hoarding raw technology. It will be won by the cognitive longevity, relentless innovation, and emotional resilience of their population. They are playing the long game and investing in their brain economy; We are falling behind.

In the military, we use a concept called staying "left of boom." It means executing proactive, aggressive conditioning and preventative strategies to stop a catastrophe before it happens, rather than digging through the wreckage after an explosion.

Right now, America’s approach to brain health is reactive. Our public policy treats brain aging as an inevitable, downhill slide into deficit. We pour billions of dollars into solving brain health collapse, like dementia and visible cognitive breakdown, before we actively intervene. But that approach is a losing strategy. We must shift from a reactive, disease-focused model to a proactive era of precision brain health in order to finally maximize American brainpower. If we do not actively optimize our collective intelligence and mental endurance, we will fall behind not only in defense readiness but also in scientific advancement and workforce productivity.

Fortunately, building a sharper, more resilient nation has never been easier or more measurable.

A landmark, three-year longitudinal study of 4,000 adults recently published in Nature Portfolio’s Scientific Reports completely dismantles the myth of inevitable cognitive decline. The data proves that the human brain possesses a no-ceiling capability. From ages 19 to 94, the brain retains a profound capacity to continually rewire, adapt, and improve its performance over time.

The key to unlocking this potential is a newly validated, multidimensional metric called the BrainHealth Index. For the first time, we can treat the brain exactly like physical fitness. We don't guess if our hearts are healthy; we measure blood pressure. The BrainHealth Index finally gives us a credible benchmark to track and measure holistic brain improvement across three critical pillars:

  • Clarity: Our raw capacity to solve complex, novel problems and drive deep technological innovation.
  • Connectedness: Our capacity for social purpose and communication, which serves as the bedrock for stable families and strong communities.
  • Emotional Balance: The mental resilience required to perform under extreme pressure, from corporate boardrooms to tactical defense environments.

When we actively invest in and train our cognitive micro-skills, the positive implications ripple across society. Every day, citizens become better in their personal relationships, more productive at their jobs, and significantly more resilient against modern burnout and life stressors. Scaled nationally, this collective mental fitness becomes the invisible armor required for our national defense and technological endurance.

As a neurologist, a retired U.S. Army Colonel, and the former founding director of DARPA’s Biological Technologies Office, I have spent my entire career protecting and restoring the brains of our service members. I know what the human mind is capable of achieving when it is pushed to optimize, rather than just manage decline.

Our federal agencies, including the Department of Health and Human Services, the NIH, and the Department of Veterans Affairs, must immediately work to adopt scalable, digital health initiatives that democratize these brain optimization tools nationwide. But executive action is only half the battle. Congress must step up and introduce a unified, bipartisan National Brain Capital Act. Just as lawmakers realized we could not secure our future without a CHIPS and Science Act to defend our artificial intelligence hardware, they must recognize that we cannot protect our nation without a legislative framework to maximize our human brainpower. We must empower every single citizen with the self-agency to improve their own cognitive capacity. It is time for Congress to stop treating brain performance as a passive medical luxury for the few. It is a national imperative to keep America leading the world.

item.title: The DC-Silicon Valley anti-China coalition is falling apart
item.description:
Arriving in the White House in 2021, President Joe Biden set about dismantling much of his predecessor’s foreign-policy agenda. But there was one clear area of continuity: China.

Here, Biden retained the first Trump administration’s confrontational approach, expanding the use of export controls on advanced technology and keeping China as the U.S. military’s pacing threat. In a time of deep political division, the newly formed China consensus appeared all-powerful. When the House voted in January 2023 to establish a select committee on “Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party,” the tally was 365 to 65.

Once President Donald Trump returned to power, observers expected more of the same. But Trump has instead moved U.S. China policy in the opposite direction, seeking to de-escalate bilateral tension in favor of “constructive strategic stability” and revealing that the bipartisan consensus on the “China threat” may be more ephemeral than many assumed.

Indeed, there is good reason to believe the peak of anti-China sentiment in U.S. politics has passed.

China’s place as the primary U.S. strategic competitor has its roots back in the early 2000s, but the narrative really took hold during Trump’s first term, when it won support from five different groups.

The first group was Trump’s Rust Belt base, to whom he and others supplied a narrative that scapegoated China for the economic and social dislocation they had suffered. China was also blamed for deaths of despair, including overdoses caused by fentanyl, whose precursor chemicals often came from China.

This groundswell against globalization was seized upon by a second group, made up of critics of the conventional economic case for global free trade: Trump himself, Peter Navarro, and Robert Lighthizer. Beginning in 2018, they imposed tariffs on some $360 billion of Chinese imports. The Biden administration maintained and entrenched this departure from free-trade globalism, announcing a “worker-centered” trade policy and reviving a U.S. industrial policy. Between them, the two administrations made bipartisan a shift away from the previous economic orthodoxy toward one focused on competitive trade with China.

The third group consisted of the foreign-policy establishment of liberal internationalists and conservative hawks. For this group, China filled a gap in U.S. foreign policy that had been empty since the end of the Cold War: the foreign adversary against which the U.S. could organize a global security bloc. In Trump’s first term, the role fell to the administration’s primacists and their allies – John Bolton, Matt Pottinger, and Mike Pompeo, who went to the Nixon Library in July 2020 to call for “a new alliance of democracies.” Two years later, Biden’s National Security Strategy called China “the only competitor with both the intent to reshape the international order and, increasingly, the economic, diplomatic, military, and technological power to advance that objective.” Accordingly, Biden and his national security team set about trying to contain Chinese power.

The fourth group contributing to the anti-China consensus were the offensive realists, such as John Mearsheimer and Elbridge Colby. Although they explicitly positioned themselves against the China hawks on both sides of the aisle who viewed the adversary through more ideological framings, they converged on a preference for slowing China’s rise. This cohort came to fear that China’s growing military capabilities and ambitions posed a direct threat to U.S. interests in East Asia. In response, they urged the United States to double down on its military investments in Asia to preserve U.S. advantages where they still existed.

Silicon Valley was the fifth and final group. Though initially skeptical of national allegiances and defense contracts, America’s technologists came around in the late 2010s, when new business interests and renewed geopolitical competition changed their calculus. In November 2017, Eric Schmidt, the former Google chief executive and a prominent Democratic donor, told an audience in Washington that China would catch up with the United States by 2020 and “dominate the industries of AI” by 2030.

Silicon Valley’s few Republicans fully embraced the geopolitical turn. Palmer Luckey founded Anduril in 2017 to build defense technology for the Pentagon. Peter Thiel and Alex Karp took Palantir public in 2020 with a filing that declared working with the Chinese Communist Party “inconsistent with our culture and mission.” Before long, this position transformed from taboo to commonplace. By the 2024 presidential election, Silicon Valley had bet on a combination of Trumpian nationalism and anti-China alarmism. There were holdouts, Nvidia and Apple among them, but they were now fighting the discourse rather than shaping it.

For much of the last decade, alignment among these groups created a seemingly unshakeable anti-China consensus. Yet the common thread was always made up of separate strands, whose unwinding should come as no surprise. Each group had its own reason for diagnosing China as a menace and has now found its own reasons to move in the other direction.

For starters, although China still receives much of the blame for the economic dislocation of American workers, it was always only one villain in the story – and the most distant. Other competitors for the same slot have come to dominate domestic discussion: migrants, “woke” elites, and other assorted culture-war enemies have all been held responsible for the plight of America’s dispossessed, displacing China as a sole focus of concern.

The trade hawks have also had to temper their zeal. The second Trump administration came in boasting about tariffs, with real trade warriors in key positions: Navarro at the White House, Jamieson Greer at USTR, Howard Lutnick at Commerce. “Liberation Day,” on April 2, 2025, was the big move. Within a week, the tariff on Chinese goods stood at 145%; but this effort hit a wall when China restricted its exports of rare earth metals. Since then, both sides have sought to de-escalate in the economic domain. The Trump administration still professes a desire for some rebalancing but has settled on a renewable trade truce as acceptable for now.

The liberal internationalists and neoconservatives continue to advocate a global containment strategy, but their influence is waning. While they still represent the largest cohort in Congress and occupy many think tank sinecures, they no longer dictate the terms of discussion. Their arguments have also started to fall flat abroad. “Allies and partners” who see relative U.S. decline are in no rush to back Washington and alienate Beijing, preferring instead to hedge.

The China threat remains central to the realist prioritizers, but they, too, have been forced to moderate their position. China’s military rise and the failed U.S. war with Iran have hastened the shift in the bilateral military balance while forcing a reevaluation of what the United States military can realistically achieve in Asia. Since the U.S. cannot afford a war with China in the medium term, realist prioritizers have started to shift the goal, from the pursuit of dominance to a “decent peace.”

Finally, the tech elite has softened somewhat on China. Jensen Huang and Nvidia were attacked in Congress, by both parties, for wanting to sell chips to China, but won the argument in the White House. The administration reversed its ban on the H20 chip in July 2025 and approved sales of the more powerful H200 in December, in exchange for a share of the revenue.

Meanwhile, the general public has decisively rejected the argument that an AI race with China requires all-out support for Silicon Valley. Polls show widespread support for AI regulation and broad opposition to the construction of data centers. American skepticism of Silicon Valley has so far eclipsed any anxiety over Chinese technological advancement.

Beyond the shifting perspectives of these five groups, the American public’s fatigue with confrontational foreign policy is also a factor. The public reaction to the war with Iran underscores the limited tolerance voters have for the disruption caused by unnecessary conflict.

None of these changes guarantees peaceful U.S.-China relations going forward. Despite recent leader-level summits filled with ceremony, the two sides continue to compete intensely in the security and economic domains. U.S.-China interactions will continue to be contentious for some time.

Still, the unraveling of the ad hoc coalition that created the apparent anti-China consensus makes any form of “new cold war” unlikely — and creates the potential for a real change in how the United States approaches China over the next decade.

item.title: Brett McGurk's account of Biden Gaza policy has a huge blind spot
item.description:
In April 2024, an Israeli drone struck a humanitarian convoy in Gaza, killing seven aid workers with World Central Kitchen, the food relief organization founded by celebrity chef Jose Andres.

A phone call between Biden and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyau days later was perhaps the closest Washington and Israel came to a rupture during the president’s term, according to Brett McGurk, the coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa in the Biden National Security Council.

At the time, intelligence indicated that Iran was preparing to launch drones and missiles at Israel in retaliation for the bombing of an Iranian consulate in Damascus on the same day as the WCK strike. “If not for the pending attack from Iran, we may have taken irreversible measures against Israel at this juncture,” McGurk writes in his recent book “Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages,” calling Biden as frustrated and angry as he’d ever seen him. But the president did not go further.

Though McGurk — one of a small group of key foreign-policy decision makers in the Biden White House — says he “wrestled” with whether cracking down on Israel was the right course of action at that time, his conclusion not to was firm.

Biden ultimately said that U.S. policy will be “determined by our assessment of Israel’s immediate action on … specific, concrete measurable steps to address civilian harm,” and days later he deployed the U.S. military to help defend Israel against the Iranian attack. “If there was a better way to end the crisis, whether at this moment or another, Biden would have taken it,” McGurk writes.

Threatening to cut off assistance and even “increasing public pressure” would have been detrimental, he insists. “It seemed to encourage those fighting against it,” He added that Tehran attacked Israel in part because it saw Washington under pressure to break with Tel Aviv.

Nearly two years after Biden shuffled out of office, McGurk is hard at work trying to paint the administration’s Gaza policy as the best response to a hopelessly complex crisis. The World Central Kitchen episode is one of many instances in which McGurk argues that public disagreements between Washington and Israel only served to strengthen their adversaries, undermining efforts to secure a ceasefire and the release of hostages held by Hamas. As a result, McGurk suggests Washington had few, if any, viable alternatives to the approach Biden and his team pursued.

While “Brink” also chronicles the regional conflicts that arose following Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, including in Iran and on the Red Sea, its central focus is McGurk’s painstaking efforts to negotiate the release of the hostages taken by Hamas on October 7. Throughout the book, he portrays any perceived daylight between the U.S. and Israel as counterproductive to his diplomatic endeavors, and places the responsibility for the prolonged conflict overwhelmingly on Hamas. But former Biden administration officials who served alongside McGurk challenge that framing, arguing that his account disregards both the potential benefits of pressuring Israel and the costs of Washington's reluctance to do so.

As one former Biden administration official said, pressure on Israel actually helped secure concessions from Hamas by giving Arab governments greater political latitude to press the militant group themselves.

"When the United States demonstrated that it was also willing to exert pressure on the party over which it had the most influence, Israel, then the Arab countries were actually able to really turn the screws," the official told RS, pointing to Egypt and Turkey's key roles in the negotiations during the Biden-Trump transition, and later in the implementation of the framework signed in October 2025.

And even when American pressure failed to advance the hostage negotiations, it could achieve other objectives. Speaking about that tense April 2024 phone call in which, according to McGurk, Biden threatened to cut off military aid, Ilan Goldenberg offered a different assessment of its consequences. Where McGurk laments the potential dangers of confronting Israel, Goldenberg, who served as a Middle East adviser to Vice President Kamala Harris, says “that is only if you view this purely as a hostage negotiation and you forget all about the Palestinian humans.”

Following this intervention, Israel agreed to the temporary reopening of the Erez Crossing, and April 2024 saw the most truckloads of humanitarian supplies enter the strip of any month between October 2023 and January 2025, according to United Nations data. This represented a “fundamental change,” according to Goldenberg, one that did not last long because Washington failed to keep up the pressure.

The narrow focus on the hostage negotiations runs throughout “Brink.” McGurk devotes considerable attention to the hostages and their families, whereas the suffering of Palestinians, while acknowledged, receives far less attention, with the devastation in Gaza —where roughly 46,000 people were killed by the time Biden left office in 2025, according to health officials in the strip — largely treated as a backdrop to his diplomatic efforts.

Whether greater American pressure could have helped bring about an earlier ceasefire — one that would have freed the hostages — remains a contentious question.

Examining Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar's conduct throughout the war, there was little evidence his willingness to reach a deal was meaningfully influenced by disagreements between Washington and Israel, said the former official who spoke with RS.

“He was singularly focused on maximizing the pain on Israel,” the official said, so it simply “doesn’t add up” that he would be responsive to outside events.

Another member of the Biden administration, speaking on condition of anonymity, argued that even if public pressure risked emboldening Hamas, Washington's reluctance to confront Netanyahu carried risks of its own, giving the Israeli prime minister latitude on how to conduct negotiations even as he seemed to want the war to continue. McGurk’s perspective instead emphasizes the times when Hamas is an intransigent negotiating partner while glossing over times when Netanyahu impedes talks.

That issue becomes particularly relevant in the author’s treatment of the failed efforts to secure a ceasefire in the summer of 2024.

In late May 2024, McGurk says, Netanyahu accepted a phased ceasefire and hostage release framework that Biden had endorsed. Hamas took more than a month to respond, a delay McGurk highlights as evidence of the group's unwillingness to compromise. “Hamas did not care at all about the plight of Gazans; it only cared about its own survival,” he wrote.

Phil Gordon, who served as Harris's national security adviser, challenged McGurk's account earlier this month, arguing Hamas's eventual response in early July represented a significant concession: the group had dropped its demand that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released.

“That felt to us like a significant step forward. Nobody was naive in thinking that this wouldn't be difficult,” Gordon recently told the Jerusalem Post.

In “Brink,” McGurk describes Hamas’s response as containing “about two dozen substantive amendments to a carefully negotiated text,” many of which were “unworkable.” The ceasefire plan was further derailed, he adds, because “new issues had also arisen.”

These “new issues” refer to Netanyahu's sudden insistence on maintaining an Israeli military presence along the recently-seized Philadelphi Corridor, on Gaza’s border with Egypt, and introducing a screening mechanism for Palestinians returning to northern Gaza. Other administration officials say these demands came during a July 4 phone call with Biden, and despite the U.S. president’s push to persuade Netanyahu to move forward with the agreement. That phone call is not specifically mentioned in “Brink.”

“In the book, Brett says the situation on the ground changed and therefore the Israelis had new requirements,” Goldenberg told RS. “That's a very coded way of saying when Biden got on the phone and said to take the deal, Bibi said no.” One Israeli former hostage negotiator has said that July 2024 represented a missed chance to secure the hostages’ release, because he “didn’t think the Philadelphi Corridor was so important that it was right to miss the window of opportunity because of it.”

The new Israeli conditions proved to not be immovable. In the eventual agreement, struck in January 2025, the IDF agreed to withdraw from the corridor, though Israel has refused to follow through on that part of the agreement.

McGurk disputes the analysis that Israeli concessions were ultimately what made the agreement possible. In a book talk at the Atlantic Council this month, he called that suggestion “totally not true” and maintained that Hamas had finally accepted terms it had rejected the previous summer, driven in part by Israel’s military victories and the death of Sinwar.

McGurk occasionally acknowledges Netanyahu was an obstacle to peace, describing the prime minister during closing stages of hostage negotiations as “the flip side of Hamas,” because he would delay potential agreements, believing that prolonging the war would strengthen his negotiating position. But this doesn’t seem to affect his thinking on whether it made sense to pressure the Israeli prime minister.

The final chapters of “Brink,” however, suggest that a change in the U.S. approach also played a decisive role in the January 2025 hostage deal. Steve Witkoff, the incoming Trump administration's Middle East envoy, joins McGurk in the final negotiations. With a deal nearly complete, Witkoff aggressively presses Netanyahu to increase the number of Palestinian prisoners who would be released in exchange for nine sick or injured civilian hostages, in the first part of a larger deal.

At one point, McGurk recounts his replacement as telling the head of Mossad “tell your prime minister this is over (...) or I’ll go out right now and say the Israelis don’t give two shits about their hostages.” Ultimately, the Israeli prime minister relented.

item.title: Houthis attack Saudi Arabia before high-stakes talks in Tehran
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis have kept up their attacks on Saudi Arabia as senior officials from the kingdom, Turkey and Pakistan are due to hold high-stakes talks with Iran in Tehran on Monday, following warnings of a return to war.

Fresh explosions rattled Riyadh overnight, along with a text message warning to residents, after the Iran-allied Houthis claimed a new attack on the Saudi capital's international airport on Sunday.

item.title: How Houthi attacks have grounded flights across Saudi Arabia
item.description:
By Gianluca Lo Nostro

Oct 26 (Reuters) - Attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have nearly emptied the skies over Riyadh this month, aviation data showed on Monday, with cancellations grounding almost nine out of every 10 scheduled flights at the Saudi capital's airport.

About 86% of scheduled flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, or 4,071 out of 4,736, were cancelled between October 8 and October 25, according to the latest data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

item.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil pumping stations, Riyadh airport as fighting intensifies
item.description:
Oct 26 (Reuters) - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they had attacked Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pumping stations and Riyadh airport, as rising hostilities choke oil supplies andthreaten to erupt into a larger conflict.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said earlier it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the capital Sanaa, including one used to fire a missile towards Riyadh that the coalition said it had intercepted.

There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks.

item.title: Officials from Mecca pact countries to meet Iranian officials in Tehran
item.description:
By Andrew Mills and Ariba Shahid

Oct 26 (Reuters) - Top officials from Mecca Pact countries Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are to meet Iran's leaders in Tehran on Monday in their first high-level contact since the kingdom became a pressure point in the wider Iran conflict.

Saudi Arabia will be represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said.

item.title: Saudi coalition says struck Houthi missile facilities after Riyadh airport attack
item.description:
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis struck several of its missile launchers and storage facilities, a spokesman said on Monday, while the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on Riyadh's international airport. 

The coalition's operation came a day after explosions rattled Saudi Arabia's capital and authorities sent text messages to residents warning them of a "hostile aerial threat" to the city, which has been heavily targeted by the Houthis in recent weeks.

item.title: The UAE has so much blood on its hands in Sudan. For its nominee to lead the UN would be an outrage | Nesrine Malik
item.description:
Lana Nusseibeh has been the face of a disastrous Emirates policy that has prolonged war and death. It is a scandal that she is even being considered

Over the past few years, you can plot the plunge into global instability not only through the unchecked assaults on international law and civilian life, but through the decline and undermining of the authority and credibility of international institutions. The latest level in this spiral is the proposed appointment of Lana Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) as the UN secretary general. Her bid has been rapidly gaining momentum and endorsements. And it has been met with outrage among the Sudanese.

Nusseibeh is the minister of state at the UAE and a former UAE ambassador to the UN. For the past three years, the country has been connected to – bear with me, this will be a long sentence – supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia in Sudan, facilitating mercenaries to fight alongside the militia (which is accused of ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity and sexual violence), and appropriating international aid infrastructure to smuggle weapons into the country.

item.title: UN raises 'ethnic cleansing' concerns over Israel's Hebron operation
item.description:
Israel's military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron, launched after a deadly attack by Palestinian gunmen, raises serious concerns of "ethnic cleansing", the United Nations warned Monday.

The municipality in Hebron, the Palestinian territory's largest city, said in a statement that 3,189 people had been forced from their homes by the ongoing operation.

item.title: Egypt parliament authorises military support to Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Egypt's parliament authorised on Monday sending military support to Saudi Arabia to defend the kingdom from attacks by Yemen's Houthis, following a request from President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.

The House of Representatives voted with a two-thirds majority in favour of "authorising President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia", according to a parliament statement.

The parliament, stacked with supporters of Sisi, had held three rare secret meetings on the matter and postponed the vote twice.

item.title: Hezbollah readies for new regional war with funds from Iran, sources say
item.description:
By Laila Bassam and Maya Gebeily

BEIRUT, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Lebanese armed group Hezbollah has spent three months preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.

The group, founded by Iran's Revolutionary Guards in 1982, has been dealt severe blows in two wars with Israel since 2024, with thousands of fighters and many of its leaders killed, and much of its arsenal destroyed.

item.title: Egypt approves military support for Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks escalate
item.description:
CAIRO, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Parliament authorised Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Monday to take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself — a move that could push Cairo more directly into the conflict between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.

Sisi had asked parliament to approve military support for Egypt's Gulf Arab ally and the world's biggest oil exporter if Riyadh requested help in fighting the Houthis, whose advances also threaten the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait — southern gateway to the Red Sea and Egypt's Suez Canal.
